papers.title: Radiation Hardness Assurance of Optical Coatings for the COMPASSO Iodine Reference
papers.abstract: The COMPASSO payload demonstrates compact iodine-based optical frequency references on the International Space Station (ISS), requiring optical windows and antireflective coatings that remain stable in the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) radiation environment. Radiation analysis was performed to quantify how trapped electrons, protons, and ions affect the fused-silica iodine cell and its coatings under mission-relevant shielding and exposure scenarios. The aim was to determine whether selected coatings meet the COMPASSO optical requirements after realistic LEO irradiation, identify degradation mechanisms linked to deposition technology and materials, and provide selection guidance for coatings used in spaceborne iodine spectroscopy and optical-clock payloads. Nominal and worst-case corpuscular environments for the ISS orbit were derived using AE8/AP8, CREME96, ESP, and ISO15390 models. Eight coating stacks produced by different deposition methods were exposed to proton and electron irradiation corresponding to the nominal and worst-case mission loads. Pre- and post-irradiation characterization included reflectance and transmittance measurements, together with visual and microscopic inspection. The tests led to the selection of a four-layer $\mathrm{Ta_2O_5/SiO_2}$ stack for the iodine cell optical window. Total ionizing dose levels for all layers of the selected coating were derived with GRAS, showing that the coating will not be affected by corpuscular radiation for years in the LEO ISS environment, including the COMPASSO mission at the ISS Bartolomeo platform.

papers.title: Statistical correlations between turbulent structures and dissipation proxies in near-Earth space: the MMS 2023-2024 unbiased magnetosheath campaign
papers.abstract: The terrestrial magnetosheath provides excellent opportunities for the experimental study of space plasma physics. Turbulence and kinetic-scale dissipation processes have been extensively studied separately. However, examining their cross-scale interplay may shed light on unsolved long-standing questions: which kinetic processes specifically dissipate the plasma turbulent fluctuations, and what drives them? In this study, we perform a statistical study of high-resolution data from the 2023-2024 unbiased campaign of the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) mission to examine correlations between local small-scale accumulation of turbulent energy and peaks of dissipation proxies. The results highlight that clear regional correlations between a vast ensemble of dissipation proxies emerge on a scale of a few ion inertial lengths. Furthermore, intermittent turbulent structures dissipate energy in a hierarchical ordering

papers.title: Towards Distributed Quantum Computing: Quantum Gate Teleportation via Satellite-Distributed Entanglement under Atmospheric Depolarization
papers.abstract: We investigate quantum gate teleportation as a primitive for satellite-enabled distributed quantum computing. In the considered architecture, a satellite distributes entangled photon pairs to two optical ground stations, which transfer the shared quantum resource to remote quantum processing units. This entanglement is then used to implement a nonlocal controlled-NOT gate between two circuit qubits located in different processors. We formulate the minimal four-qubit protocol, consisting of two network qubits that provide the entangled resource and two circuit qubits on which the distributed gate is performed. Atmospheric propagation effects in the gravitational field are modeled through an effective two-qubit depolarizing channel whose parameters depend on atmospheric and optical quantities, including the Fried parameter and receiver aperture. The performance of the protocol is quantified by the fidelity between the ideal CNOT output state and the state produced by noisy quantum gate teleportation. Our results show that the fidelity is governed by the quality of the distributed entanglement and depends jointly on atmospheric coherence, aperture size, and effective depolarization strength. These findings connect physical-layer modeling of satellite optical channels with gate-level performance in distributed quantum computing.

papers.title: General Relativistic and Non-Inertial Effects on Magnetic Reconnection Rates
papers.abstract: We develop a gauge-independent theory of magnetic reconnection beyond the standard special-relativistic framework of inertial systems in flat spacetime. Our definitions of reconnection and its rate are independent of reference frame and coordinate system, allowing physical effects of gravity and net linear acceleration to be distinguished from coordinate effects. We extend the mesoscale theory of Liu et al. [PRL 118, 085101 (2017)], in which the reconnection rate depends on physics both within the diffusion region and in an upstream ideal, force-free region. The theory identifies three non-inertial and curved-spacetime (NICS) effects, including gravitationally induced magnetic tension: gravitational distortion of the reconnection plane changes the curvature of magnetic field lines. Applying the theory to a simplified accretion plasma near )a compact object, we find that (1) whether gravity increases or decreases the reconnection rate depends on the system's orientation relative to the gravitational source, with the greatest increase occurring when the outflow jet points toward or away from the source; and (2) the magnitude of the gravitational effect scales with the dimensionless parameter $\bar{\kappa} \equiv r_s\Delta y^2/r^3$, where $r$ is the Schwarzschild radial coordinate, $r_s$ is the source's Schwarzschild radius, and $\Delta y$ is the mesoscale length.

papers.title: The Role of Precursors and MHD Instabilities in Distinguishing Confined and Eruptive Solar Flares
papers.abstract: Identifying pre-flare magnetic conditions that determine whether a flare will be eruptive (associated with a coronal mass ejection) or confined remains a major challenge in solar physics. Motivated by previous statistical results showing that some eruptive flares occur under ideal MHD-stable conditions, we investigate the roles of kink instability (KI), torus instability (TI), preflare reconnection traced by precursor brightenings (PBs) and magnetic nonpotentiality in solar eruptiveness using an expanded sample of 68 flares above GOES class M4 from 2011--2024. To characterize the nonpotentiality of each active region (AR), we calculate the relative helicity $H_R$, current-carrying helicity $H_J$ and free magnetic energy. We find that, (1) 17 of 18 TI-unstable events and 12 of 19 KI-unstable events are eruptive, indicating that the TI parameter outperforms the KI parameter (2) although PBs are more commonly found in the MHD-unstable regime, only 3 of the 12 eruptive events in the TI/KI-stable regime show PBs, suggesting that preflare reconnection may play a secondary role compared with other factors. (3) The strongest indicator of eruptiveness is obtained by combining the TI parameter with magnetic nonpotentiality. Specifically, 24 of 36 eruptive flares satisfy $\sqrt{\left| H_J \right|}/\phi \geq 0.1$ or $n \geq 1.13$, whereas 24 of 25 confined flares satisfy $\sqrt{\left| H_J \right|}/\phi \le 0.1$ and $n \le 1.13$, where $\phi$ is the total unsigned magnetic flux and $n$ is the decay index. These results suggest that the overall magnetic environment of ARs may play a significant role in determining the eruptiveness, in addition to the effect of MHD instability and reconnection.

papers.title: C$_2$ Swan, CH and CN emission, surface temperature and luminous efficiency of the Hayabusa2 sample-return capsule from ground-based spectroscopy
papers.abstract: The Hayabusa2 sample-return capsule entered the atmosphere over South Australia on 5 December 2020 at 12 km/s. A slitless spectral video, taken from the ground with a hand-tracked consumer camera, shows the capsule alone from 80 to 49 km. In the first ten seconds of heating the shock layer emits the CN violet system, the CH A-X band and the C$_2$ Swan bands, the latter for the first time in remote observations of a capsule entry. C$_2$ ($T_{\rm rot}\approx9200$ K, $T_{\rm vib}\approx7800$ K) and CN (about 7000 K) are far hotter than the surface. C$_2$ and CH disappear while the heat flux is still rising and CN persists, which we relate to the early pyrolysis of the carbon-phenolic ablator and to the changing boundary-layer chemistry. The colour temperature of the heat shield rises from 2720 to 3080 K, in agreement with airborne results. The radiated energy is one to two orders of magnitude below that of natural fireballs, because the light comes from the hot surface rather than from ablation vapour. A faint persistent train lights up about 1 s after the passage and fades within a few seconds, probably chemiluminescence in the cooling wake.
